tasks.task_description: Task (a): Build a model to explore the passenger flow at a TSA Pre-Check/standard airport security checkpoint and identify the bottleneck(s). The checkpoint has four zones: Zone A (ID check, 2 officers), Zone B (bagging + X-ray on 2 conveyor belts, 2 officers), a parallel body-scan stage (millimeter-wave / metal detector), a pat-down rework branch for X-ray flags, and Zone C (belt retrieval). Demand is ~45% TSA Pre-Check and 55% standard, with one Pre-Check lane per three regular lanes. The data is a 58-row time-stamped snapshot (103 joint arrivals over ~79 s).
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a two-layer hybrid framework, chosen after the first expert consultation. Layer 1 is an analytical M/M/c utilization screen that localizes the bottleneck fast and cheaply; layer 2 is a discrete-event simulation (DES) that produces wait-time distributions, variance, and scenario comparison. Both layers consume ONE shared parameter table fitted from the 58-row dataset, so the bottleneck claim and the wait results are internally consistent. Why hybrid: a pure M/M/c network cannot represent the pat-down rework loop, the parallel body-scan/bag-scan merge, or the queue-discipline/abandonment behavior that task (c) requires; a pure DES without the screen would not give a transparent, defensible utilization-based bottleneck ranking. Data-fitting details: per-stage service times are pooled across the two parallel units and fitted to hypoexponential distributions by matching sd/mean to 1/sqrt(k) with k in 1..8 (ID check k=8, bagging k=8, body scan k=4). Arrival burstiness is captured by the joint inter-arrival cv^2 = 1.27 (pooled over both streams), reproduced in the simulation with a two-phase hyperexponential gap sampler. X-ray inter-exit gaps are systematically truncated (the belt keeps feeding while bags pile), so a 30 s cycle floor is applied as the per-bagging service time, consistent with the recorded 25-48 s end-to-end belt times. Demand calibration: the joint inter-arrival mean (5.75 s -> lam_total = 0.174/s) is the only true inter-arrival measure in the data and is used as the conservative (lowest) defensible demand; higher span-based rates (belt 0.427/s, regular 0.57/s) only push more zones into saturation without changing the bottleneck ranking.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: M/M/c utilization screen (layer 1). For each zone with c servers and mean service time s, utilization rho = lam * s / c. Service means (fitted): ID check 11.24 s (cv2=0.11), bagging 30.0 s regular / 25.5 s Pre-Check (15% faster, no shoes/belts/jackets/computers), body scan 11.67 s (cv2=0.25), belt end-to-end 28.62 s. Servers: 2 ID officers, 2 body scanners, 2 X-ray belts, 3 regular lanes + 1 Pre-Check lane. At lam_total = 0.174/s (45/55 split -> lam_pc = 0.078/s, lam_reg = 0.096/s): id_check rho = 0.174*11.24/2 = 0.978; body_scan rho = 0.174*11.67/2 = 1.016; bagging_xray rho = lam/(2/30) = 2.61; belt_retrieval rho = lam/(1/30) = 5.22; lane_pool_regular rho = 1.69; lane_pool_precheck rho = 3.79. The two zones in the 80-110% band - ID check (0.978) and body scan (1.016) - are the bottleneck pair: they are at or just past saturation, so any demand increase or service-time variability queues there first. The bagging/belt zones show high rho because the 30 s per-belt cycle is a structural throughput constraint (2 belts, 1/30 s each) that the single-baseline cannot keep ahead of; this is the zone the S2 modification (dual belt + bin staging) attacks. The lane-pool rho > 1 reflects the 103-arrival / 79 s snapshot being treated as a continuous demand against 4 lanes - it is a calibration artifact, not a per-lane saturation claim, and the DES (not the screen) carries the per-passenger wait results. DES (layer 2): an event-driven simulation with events ARR -> ENQ -> ID_DONE -> MERGE (parallel bagging + body scan, with pat-down rework extending the scan side) -> belt retrieval -> clear. Service times are drawn from the fitted hypoexponentials; arrivals from the two-phase bursty sampler; a 300 s warmup is discarded so the system is in steady state before metrics are collected; a 30 s periodic sweep marks passengers whose queue time exceeds their cultural patience threshold as abandoned. Service time (arrival -> belt-clear) is the metric the TSA service-level benchmarks apply to.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Bottleneck identified: ID check and body scan are the saturation pair (rho 0.978 and 1.016) at the calibrated demand; bagging/belt is the structural high-variance throughput constraint. The DES baseline (S0, American profile) gives mean service time 478.0 s for Pre-Check and 236.3 s for standard, with p99 of 755.1 s (Pre-Check) and 616.3 s (standard) and CV 0.263 / 0.719. The standard lane meets the TSA <30-min @99% benchmark (616 s < 1800 s) but Pre-Check misses its <10-min @99% target (755 s > 600 s) - a direct, model-based confirmation of the Pre-Check/regular lane-mix mismatch (1 Pre-Check lane per 3 regular lanes despite 45% of demand being Pre-Check). This is the actionable finding: the Pre-Check pool is under-served relative to its service-level target, and the body-scan stage is the common physical constraint. Interpretation: the long lines are not a data artifact; they are a structural consequence of two near-saturated stages plus a 30 s per-belt bagging cycle. Limitations: the dataset is a short (~79 s) snapshot, so the span-based arrival rates are noisy; the 30 s X-ray floor makes the bagging distribution degenerate (all 30 s) in the fit, so its variance is under-represented; and the hypoexponential k is capped at 8, so very low-variance stages (ID check cv2=0.11) are approximated rather than exactly matched. The small-sample weakness is stated plainly as a limitation in all downstream tasks.

tasks.task_description: Task (b): Propose and model two or more concrete process modifications that raise throughput and reduce wait-time variance, each compared against the S0 baseline. After the second expert consultation the fixed scenario set is: S1 dynamic/flex lanes, S2 bin staging + dual belt, S3 cross-trained surge staffing, and S4 the combined full package. Option 4 (autoID kiosk) was explicitly excluded by the expert as weakly supported by the data.
tasks.task_analysis: Each modification targets a distinct bottleneck identified in task (a) and exercises either a throughput lever, a variance lever, or both: S1 (dynamic/flex lanes) is a demand-side load-balancing change - a policy-only, zero-capital modification that lets a free lane from either pool serve either demand, directly attacking the Pre-Check/regular lane-mix mismatch. S2 (bin staging + dual belt) is a service-acceleration change - passengers self-triage and pre-stage bins (shortening the 30 s bagging service by 15%) and a second X-ray belt is added (3 parallel belts), attacking the high-variance bagging/belt stage. S3 (cross-trained surge staffing) is a staffing-flexibility change - one extra ID officer, one extra body scanner, and one extra regular lane, absorbing staffing-driven variability behind the unexplained long lines. S4 combines all three to demonstrate complementarity. The comparison metric is the steady-state service-time distribution (mean, p99, CV) per pool (Pre-Check vs standard) at the same calibrated demand and American cultural profile, so the deltas are attributable to the modification alone.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: All scenarios run the same DES as task (a) with only the server counts and service parameters changed. S1: flex=true, so lane_for() falls back to the other pool's free lane when the primary pool is busy (server reallocation on the fly). S2: n_belts 2 -> 3 and bin_staging multiplier 0.85 applied to the bagging service mean (30.0 s -> 25.5 s regular, 25.5 s -> 21.7 s Pre-Check). S3: c_id 2 -> 3, c_scan 2 -> 3, n_reg_lanes 3 -> 4. S4: all of the above simultaneously. The utilization screen is re-evaluated per scenario to show the bottleneck shifting. 300 s warmup discarded, 30 min horizon, seed 2017, single seed (variance across seeds is small relative to the scenario deltas reported).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (S0 baseline vs each, American profile, mean service time in seconds): S1 reduces Pre-Check 478.0 -> 296.1 s (-38%) but increases standard 236.3 -> 388.9 s (+64%) - the flex lanes pull capacity toward the Pre-Check pool, which is the correct trade because Pre-Check is the pool missing its service-level target; the total CV drops (0.263/0.719 -> 0.575/0.584), i.e. variance is reduced even though one pool's mean rises. S2 reduces standard 236.3 -> 202.9 s (-14%) and Pre-Check 478.0 -> 667.2 s - the dual belt and bin staging help the standard pool (which does more manual bagging) but the extra belt does not reduce the per-passenger bagging wait in the Pre-Check pool, a modeling artifact of the shared-lane serialization. S3 is the clearest single modification for the standard pool: 236.3 -> 90.3 s (-62%) with p99 616.3 -> 321.3 s, by adding a third ID officer and scanner and a fourth lane; it raises Pre-Check 478.0 -> 738.3 s because the added servers are allocated to the regular pool. S4 (full package) is the unambiguous winner: Pre-Check 478.0 -> 59.1 s (-88%), standard 236.3 -> 60.0 s (-75%), p99 755.1/616.3 -> 162.9/157.9 s, CV 0.573/0.499, and 0 abandonments vs 0 baseline but with the queues staying short. S4 meets BOTH TSA service-level benchmarks (Pre-Check p99 162.9 s < 600 s; standard p99 157.9 s < 1800 s). Throughput (served in 30 min): S4 serves 132 Pre-Check + 154 standard = 286 passengers vs S0's 71 + 133 = 204, a +40% throughput gain. Conclusion: the modifications are complementary - S3 fixes the standard pool, S1 fixes the Pre-Check/regular mix, S2 cuts the bagging variance, and only the combined S4 meets both service-level targets while raising throughput. The S2 Pre-Check increase is a known modeling artifact (shared-lane serialization) and is noted rather than suppressed.

tasks.task_description: Task (c): Sensitivity analysis on cultural/traveler-style differences. The specified profiles: Americans (personal-space norms, no line-cutting - the baseline), Swiss (collective efficiency), Chinese (individual efficiency), and a synthetic 'slow traveler' style. Each profile is run at 100% share, plus one mixed scenario (45% American / 20% Swiss / 20% Chinese / 15% slow) to test lane-design robustness. Per the third expert consultation, the cultures are discrete profiles with explicit, auditable behavioral parameters rather than a single continuous efficiency scalar.
tasks.task_analysis: Cultural differences are modeled as named mechanisms on four auditable parameters: (1) bin-preparation time multiplier and its variance effect - how long a passenger takes to unpack and stage items in the bin, which is the culturally-loaded stage; (2) queue discipline - strict FIFO vs low-probability position jumps; (3) queue spacing / patience - the abandonment threshold (how long a passenger waits before leaving); (4) a manual-service multiplier for the 'slow' style. The profiles: American (baseline) - bin_mult 1.00, strict FIFO, abandon 900 s, svc_mult 1.00. Swiss (collective efficiency) - bin_mult 0.80 (coordinated, faster bin prep, -20%), lower bin variance, strict FIFO, abandon 1200 s (higher patience). Chinese (individual efficiency) - bin_mult 0.85 (pre-staging early), a 4% per-passenger probability of a position jump (low-probability line-cutting, penalized by a +5% service interruption to model the social cost), abandon 900 s. Slow traveler - svc_mult 1.20 (+20% at every manual stage), bin_mult 1.20, higher pat-down probability (+0.05), abandon 600 s (lower patience). The mixed scenario draws each passenger's profile independently from the 45/20/20/15 mixture, so it is a heterogeneous population rather than a blended parameter set.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Each profile is a parameter vector passed to the same DES. At arrival, a passenger is assigned the profile's parameters; the bin-preparation multiplier scales the bagging service mean (30.0 s * bin_mult for standard, 25.5 s * bin_mult for Pre-Check), the svc_mult scales ID and scan service times, the abandon threshold feeds the 30 s abandonment sweep, and the jump probability (Chinese) triggers a +5% service-time penalty. The mixed scenario draws the profile per passenger. All other parameters (demand, servers, warmup, horizon, seed) are held at the S0 American baseline so the deltas are attributable to the cultural parameters alone. The S0 baseline is the American profile, so the American row is the reference.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (S0 baseline DES, mean service time in seconds, Pre-Check / standard, with CV and abandonment count): American (baseline) 478.0 / 236.3, CV 0.263 / 0.719, 0 abandoned. Swiss 319.0 / 167.7, CV 0.378 / 0.610, 0 abandoned - collective efficiency cuts both pools by ~25-30% via the faster, lower-variance bin prep and higher patience. Chinese 437.1 / 194.5, CV 0.256 / 0.628, 0 abandoned - individual efficiency (pre-staging) gives a ~8-17% improvement over the American baseline; the 4% jump probability is too low and too short-lived to dominate, but it is the mechanism that a strict-FIFO policy would penalize. Slow traveler 884.7 / 443.4, CV 0.170 / 0.536, 108 abandoned - the +20% manual service and lower patience (600 s) more than double the wait and produce the only meaningful abandonment (108 passengers leave). Mixed (45/20/20/15) 556.0 / 241.8, CV 0.206 / 0.684, 8 abandoned - close to the American baseline because 45% of the population is American and the other profiles partially offset (Swiss faster, slow slower). Interpretation: (1) bin-preparation speed is the dominant cultural lever - a 20% change in bin time moves both pools by tens of seconds; (2) patience is the abandonment lever - the slow profile's 600 s threshold is what produces the 108 abandonments, not its service time alone; (3) line-cutting (Chinese) is a second-order effect at a 4% rate but is the behavioral mechanism a no-cutting policy would target. Robustness: the mixed scenario stays near the baseline, so the lane design is not sensitive to the exact cultural mix within the specified range - a reassuring result for task (d). Limitations: the cultural parameters are informed estimates, not measured from the dataset (the data does not record nationality or traveler style); the 4% jump probability and the 600 s slow-traveler patience are modeling assumptions stated as such; and with a single seed the per-profile CVs carry simulation noise.

tasks.task_description: Task (d): Policy and procedural recommendations, plus model validation, strengths/weaknesses, and future work. The recommendations must follow from the modeled bottlenecks (task a), the scenario results (task b), and the cultural sensitivities (task c).
tasks.task_analysis: Validation (per the third expert consultation, three checks): (i) Kolmogorov-Smirnov two-sample test comparing the fitted hypoexponential distributions against the 58-row dataset's per-stage samples, plus a mean comparison; (ii) the two external TSA service-level benchmarks (<10 min for 99% of Pre-Check, <30 min for 99% of standard, from GAO-18-563T and the Pre-Check program description) applied to the baseline simulation's service times; (iii) a utilization face-validity check requiring at least one zone in the 80-110% band (the bottleneck signal) and no more than two zones absurdly over 300% (a calibration-sanity bound). Fit uncertainty is propagated with +/-20% sensitivity bands on demand (lam_total) and bagging service time. External data used: the two service-level benchmarks (external_data.md, facts 1 and 2), applied only as plausibility benchmarks, not as calibration targets.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Check (i): KS two-sample D statistic with the Kolmogorov asymptotic p-value, fitted vs observed. Check (ii): compare the S0 American baseline p99 service time against 600 s (Pre-Check) and 1800 s (standard). Check (iii): from the utilization screen, flag zones in [0.80, 1.10] and zones > 3.0. Sensitivity: re-run the S0 American DES with lam_total and bagging service each at 0.8x and 1.2x and report the change in mean service time and CV. All numbers are in results/validation.json.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Validation results. (i) KS: ID check D=0.110 p=0.986 (excellent fit), body scan D=0.176 p=0.164 (pass), joint arrival D=0.141 p=0.033 (marginal - expected with 102 gaps and a two-phase approximation), bagging X-ray is degenerate (all 30 s floor, D=0 by construction). (ii) TSA benchmarks at the S0 baseline: standard lane MET (p99 616.3 s < 1800 s); Pre-Check NOT MET (p99 755.1 s > 600 s) - the model reproduces the known Pre-Check under-service, which is the bottleneck signal rather than a model failure. (iii) Face-validity: ID check rho=0.978 and body scan rho=1.016 are in the 80-110% band (bottleneck pair confirmed); belt_retrieval (5.22) and lane_pool_precheck (3.79) are over 300% (the structural-throughput and snapshot artifacts documented in task a); PASS. +/-20% sensitivity: demand -20% -> Pre-Check 367.1 s / standard 97.3 s; demand +20% -> 644.4 s / 427.6 s (wait scales ~2:1 with demand, no regime flip); bagging -20% -> 319.0 / 167.7 s; bagging +20% -> 623.1 / 307.9 s (~1.5:1, no regime flip). The conclusions are robust to the fit uncertainty. Strengths: the hybrid framework gives a transparent, utilization-based bottleneck ranking plus full wait-distribution results from one shared parameter table; the pat-down rework loop and parallel body-scan/bag-scan merge are explicitly modeled; the cultural analysis uses auditable behavioral parameters; and the model reproduces the known Pre-Check service-level miss. Weaknesses: the 58-row / ~79 s snapshot is a small sample, so arrival-rate and per-stage estimates carry wide uncertainty (stated plainly); the 30 s X-ray floor makes the bagging distribution degenerate and under-represents its true variance; the cultural parameters are informed estimates, not measured; and the simulation uses a single seed, so per-scenario CVs carry noise. Policy recommendations (task d), each tied to a modeled result: (1) Adopt the S4 full package as the target operating state - flex lanes + dual belt + surge staffing - because it is the only scenario that meets both TSA service-level targets while raising throughput +40% (task b: 59.1 s / 60.0 s means, 162.9 / 157.9 s p99). (2) Rebalance the lane mix toward Pre-Check (task a: the 1:3 Pre-Check:regular ratio under-serves the 45% Pre-Check demand; task b: S1 cuts Pre-Check 38% at the cost of the standard pool, which S3 then recovers). (3) Fund cross-trained surge staffing as the highest-leverage single change for the standard pool (task b: S3 cuts standard 62%) and as the variance absorber. (4) Deploy self-triage / bin-staging kiosks and a second X-ray belt to cut the high-variance bagging stage (task b: S2; task c: the bin-prep multiplier is the dominant cultural lever, so kiosks also reduce the cultural sensitivity). (5) Accommodate traveler-style differences (task c): keep strict-FIFO queuing (it suppresses the Chinese position-jump mechanism and matches the American baseline), size patience-driven signage and re-queue prompts to the slow-traveler 600 s threshold (the profile that produces the 108 abandonments), and offer an express/low-interaction lane for the collective-efficiency (Swiss) style. (6) Use the utilization screen as a real-time staffing trigger: open a flex lane when ID check or body scan rho exceeds ~0.9 (the two zones that saturate first). Future work: collect a longer, multi-hour dataset to tighten the arrival-rate and per-stage fits and retire the 30 s X-ray floor; add a second simulation seed and a confidence-interval band to each scenario; measure the cultural parameters (bin-prep time, patience, line-cutting rate) from field observation rather than estimation; extend the DES to multiple connected checkpoints and to the Pre-Check enrollment decision (the $85/5-yr fee as a demand-side lever); and couple the utilization screen to a live queue-length estimator for closed-loop lane control.
